To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic alcohol abuse induces a number of pathological changes in organs outside of the liver, including intestinal epithelial cell dysfunction, adipose tissue inflammation, skeletal muscle atrophy, and kidney injury, that are important drivers of liver disease progression.
Chronic alcohol abuse initiates multiple interorgan cross-talk pathways that lead to liver injury.

(i) alcohol-induced gut leakiness leads to increased bacterial translocation, which in turn drives systemic inflammation and end-organ injury; (ii) alcohol-induced gut dysbiosis leads to increased gut permeability and increased gut-derived bacterial products; (iii) alcohol-induced gut injury leads to increased gut-derived endotoxin and other proinflammatory bacterial products; and (iv) alcohol-induced gut microbiome changes lead to an increase in the production of proinflammatory bacterial metabolites.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of chronic alcohol abuse on the intestine and the role of the intestinal microbiome in the progression of ALH.
understanding how alcohol’s effects outside the liver contribute to the progression of alcoholic liver disease.
the effects of alcohol on nonhepatic organs and how those effects contribute to ALD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alcohol abuse causes a multitude of changes in multiple organ systems.
the liver is not the only organ affected by chronic alcohol exposure, and the effects of alcohol on other organs contribute substantially to the development of ALD.
the liver is not the only target for alcohol and that alcohol’s effects on the liver are only one part of a larger story that is just beginning to unfold.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of alcohol are not confined to the liver.
alcohol’s effects are not just confined to the liver, and in fact, the effects of alcohol on other organs are likely the most important contributors to the progression of liver injury.
alcohol abuse causes multiple organ injury, which leads to the development of a systemic inflammatory state that drives liver injury and progression to end-stage disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
alcohol abuse initiates multiple organ dysfunctions that ultimately contribute to liver disease.
ALD is a systemic disease, not a liver-specific disease, and that alcohol-induced organ damage is a key component of ALD progression.
the liver does not exist in a vacuum, but rather is intimately linked to other organ systems.
